md:
### Dissection classifications at a glance

| System | Based on | Categories | Use and limits |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stanford | Extent: is the ascending aorta involved? | A involves the ascending aorta (DeBakey I and II); B does not (DeBakey IIIa and IIIb), whatever the entry site | Binary; cannot separate subgroups with different outcomes |
| DeBakey | Extent | I ascending and beyond (60%); II ascending only (10 to 15%); IIIa descending thoracic, IIIb below the diaphragm (III 25 to 30%) | DeBakey II patients will probably be left without structural aortic wall disease after surgery |
| Non-A non-B | Extent | Arch involved, ascending spared: dissection confined to the arch, or retrograde from the descending aorta into the arch | 30-day mortality about 14% medically treated, 4.4% after successful surgery; surgery or endovascular therapy favoured within 14 days |
| SVS/STS 2020 | Entry tear zone, with proximal (P) and distal (D) extent by zones 0 to 12 | A_D: entry in zone 0. B_PD: entry in zone 1 or beyond. I_D: entry unidentified, involving zone 0 | Guides decisions on sealing the entry tear |
| TEM | Type, Entry, Malperfusion | Type A, B or non-A non-B; E0 to E3 (none seen, ascending, arch, descending); M0 to M3 (none, coronary, supra-aortic, spinal, visceral or iliac), each (−) or (+) clinical | More prognostic information; recommended by EACTS/STS for any acute aortic syndrome (IIa, C) |
| Penn (type A) | Ischaemia at presentation | Aa none (about 5% mortality); Ab branch malperfusion; Ac circulatory collapse; Abc both | Odds of death against Aa: 2.4, 3.4 and 13.1 |

Source: summarised from this section (ESC 2024 sections 9.3.1 to 9.3.1.1.3) and the EACTS/STS 2024 classification and risk score section of this tab.

md:
### Cerebral protection options at a glance

| Strategy | How | Limits and timing | What the notes say about evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deep hypothermic arrest alone | Arrest at 18 to 22 °C, no cerebral perfusion | Safe up to about 30 min (EACTS/STS); 18 °C gives 30 to 40 min (TSRA). Lengthens bypass; coagulopathy, inflammation, organ dysfunction | Has given way to RCP or ACP. STS (6387 type A): ACP or RCP gave lower death and stroke than arrest without cerebral perfusion |
| Retrograde cerebral perfusion | Perfuse up the superior vena cava during arrest | Hemiarch with arrest about 30 min: results similar to antegrade (EACTS/STS) | RCT in elective arch: no difference from ACP in stroke, MRI or neurocognition. TSRA: adds nothing to deep arrest alone |
| Unilateral antegrade (ACP) | Right axillary or subclavian inflow, clamp the innominate | Arrest under 40 min: unilateral or bilateral both reasonable | Meta-analysis of 4 strategies: unilateral perfusion in moderate hypothermia best for in-hospital mortality and stroke (only 40% total arch) |
| Bilateral antegrade | Add left carotid perfusion | Arrest over 40 min: bilateral from the start; NIRS can guide the switch | No proven advantage over unilateral (AATS 2021); bilateral may be better with arrest over 30 to 50 min (ACC/AHA 2022) |
| Trilateral antegrade | Also perfuse the left subclavian (cannulation or intubation) | Incomplete circle of Willis on preoperative CTA | EACTS/STS 2024 IIa, C |
| Temperature with ACP | Lower-body arrest at high-moderate hypothermia (core 24.1 to 28 °C) | Hemiarch: with cerebral perfusion (I, C). Complex arch: with selective ACP (IIa, B) | With ACP, moderate hypothermia appears as safe as deep; Manoly meta-analysis: lower mortality and stroke than deep |
| Monitoring | Bilateral NIRS with an algorithm for desaturation | All arch repair | EACTS/STS 2024 I, C |

Source: summarised from the EACTS/STS 2024 organ protection section (part 2), the ACC/AHA 2022 and AATS 2021 type A sections and the TSRA textbook account in this tab.

md:
### IMH and PAU side by side

| Feature | Intramural haematoma | Penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer |
|---|---|---|
| Share of AAS | 5 to 25% | 2 to 7% |
| Lesion | Haemorrhage from the vasa vasorum within the media, with or without intimal disruption | Plaque ulcer through the internal elastic lamina into the media; often with IMH |
| Usual site | DTA 60 to 70%, ascending about 30%, arch about 10% | Mid and lower DTA; ascending rarely, but there (especially with IMH) rupture risk 33 to 75% |
| Typical patient | Older than classic dissection; similar risk factors and symptoms | Older male smoker over 65 with hypertension, CAD, COPD, renal impairment, AAA |
| Imaging | Crescentic or circular wall thickening, no flap, no enhancement after contrast; TTE sensitivity under 40% | CT technique of choice; often multiple, 5 to 25 mm wide, 4 to 30 mm deep |
| High-risk features | Diameter over 45 to 50 mm (A) or 47 to 50 mm (B); thickness over 10 mm (A) or 13 mm (B); ulcer-like projection; effusion; malperfusion; uncontrolled pain or BP | Width 13 to 20 mm or more; depth 10 mm or more; growth over 5 mm a year; saccular aneurysm; increasing pleural effusion |
| Type A | Urgent surgery (I, C); wait and see in selected high-risk patients without high-risk features (IIb, C) | Surgery (I, C); same wait-and-see exception (IIb, C) |
| Uncomplicated type B | Medical therapy, repeat CT or CMR (I, C); TEVAR if high-risk imaging features (IIa, C) | Medical therapy, repeat imaging (I, C); endovascular if high-risk imaging features (IIa, C) |
| Complicated type B | TEVAR (I, C); surgery if anatomy unfavourable (IIb, C) | TEVAR (I, C); surgery by anatomy and comorbidity (IIb, C) |
| Follow-up if medical | 1, 3, 6 and 12 months, then yearly (as type B dissection) | 1 month, then every 6 months; longer after 2 stable years |
| Outcome | In-hospital mortality type A 26.6%, type B 4.4% | Early aortic mortality 7.2% endovascular against 15.9% open |

Source: summarised from this section (ESC 2024 sections 9.3.2 to 9.3.3, Table 16, Recommendation Tables 51, 52 and 54).

md:
### Chronic type B dissection: open repair against TEVAR

| | Open repair | TEVAR |
|---|---|---|
| Where it fits | First line in low-risk patients and in HTAD; STS/AATS: consider open repair unless comorbidity is prohibitive or anatomy unsuitable for TEVAR | Preferred for eligible chronic TBAD; suitable for high-risk patients unfit for open repair |
| Early mortality | 6 to 11% (up to 20% in low-volume centres: centralise) | Under 5% |
| Spinal cord ischaemia | 3 to 11% | Under 3% (stroke also under 3%) |
| Meta-analysis | More durable | Lower early mortality, stroke, SCI and respiratory complications; more re-interventions; long-term survival similar |
| Limits | Technically harder than degenerative aneurysm because of the flap | False-lumen thrombosis usually only above the coeliac trunk: lifelong distal surveillance. Left subclavian cover often needed, with revascularisation. TEVAR alone discouraged with abdominal enlargement, poor distal landing or large re-entry tears |
| When to treat (both) | Descending diameter 60 mm or more at reasonable surgical risk (I, B); 55 mm or more at low procedural risk (IIa, C); emergency for malperfusion, rupture or progression (I, C) | |

Source: summarised from this section (ESC 2024 section 9.3.1.4.5 and Recommendation Table 50).
